{{Short description|In algebra, completion w.r.t. powers of an ideal}}
{{Other uses|Completeness (disambiguation){{!}}Completeness}}
In [[abstract algebra]], a '''completion''' is any of several related [[functor]]s on [[ring (mathematics)|rings]] and [[module (mathematics)|modules]] that result in complete [[topological ring]]s and [[topological module|modules]]. Completion is similar  to [[localization of a ring|localization]], and together they are among the most basic tools in analysing [[commutative ring]]s. Complete commutative rings have a simpler structure than general ones, and [[Hensel's lemma]] applies to them. In [[algebraic geometry]], a completion of a ring of functions ''R'' on a space ''X'' concentrates on a '''formal neighborhood''' of a point of ''X'': heuristically, this is a neighborhood so small that ''all'' [[Taylor series]] centered at the point are convergent. An algebraic completion is constructed in a manner analogous to [[complete metric space|completion]] of a [[metric space]] with [[Cauchy sequence]]s, and agrees with it in the case when ''R'' has a metric given by a [[ultrametric space|non-Archimedean]] [[absolute value (algebra)|absolute value]].

== General construction ==

Suppose that ''E'' is an [[abelian group]] with a descending [[filtration (mathematics)|filtration]]

: <math>E = F^0 E \supset F^1 E \supset F^2 E \supset \cdots \,</math>

of subgroups. One then defines the completion (with respect to the filtration) as the [[inverse limit]]:

: <math>\widehat{E} = \varprojlim (E/F^n E)=\left\{\left.(\overline{a_n})_{n\geq0} \in \prod_{n\geq0}(E/F^nE) \;\right|\; a_i \equiv a_j\pmod{F^iE} \text{ for all } i \leq j\right\}. \,</math>

This is again an abelian group. Usually ''E'' is an ''additive'' abelian group. If ''E'' has additional algebraic structure compatible with the filtration, for instance ''E'' is a [[filtered algebra|filtered ring]], a filtered [[module (mathematics)|module]], or a filtered [[vector space]], then its completion is again an object with the same structure that is complete in the topology determined by the filtration. This construction may be applied both to [[commutative ring|commutative]] and [[noncommutative ring]]s. As may be expected, when the intersection of the <math>F^i E</math> equals zero, this produces a [[Topological_ring#Completion|complete topological ring]].

== Krull topology ==
{{Main|Adic topology}}
In [[commutative algebra]], the filtration on a [[commutative ring]] ''R'' by the powers of a proper [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] ''I'' determines the Krull (after [[Wolfgang Krull]]) or ''I''-[[adic topology]] on ''R''. The case of a [[maximal ideal|''maximal'' ideal]] <math>I=\mathfrak{m}</math> is especially important, for example the distinguished maximal ideal of a [[valuation ring]]. The [[basis of open neighbourhoods]] of 0 in ''R'' is given by the powers ''I''<sup>''n''</sup>, which are ''nested'' and form a descending filtration on ''R'':
<!-- nested: ''I''<sup>''n''</sup>⊃''I''<sup>''n''+1</sup>-->

:<math> F^0 R = R\supset I\supset I^2\supset\cdots, \quad F^n R = I^n.</math>

(Open neighborhoods of any ''r'' &isin; ''R'' are given by cosets ''r'' + ''I''<sup>''n''</sup>.) The (''I''-adic) completion is the [[inverse limit]] of the [[factor ring]]s,

: <math> \widehat{R}_I=\varprojlim (R/I^n) </math>

pronounced "R I hat". The kernel of the canonical map {{pi}} from the ring to its completion is the intersection of the powers of ''I''. Thus {{pi}} is injective if and only if this intersection reduces to the zero element of the ring; by the [[Krull intersection theorem]], this is the case for any commutative [[Noetherian ring]] which is an [[integral domain]] or a [[local ring]].

There is a related topology on ''R''-[[module (mathematics)|modules]], also called Krull or ''I''-adic topology. A basis of open neighborhoods of a module ''M'' is given by the sets of the form

:<math>x + I^n M \quad\text{for }x \in M.</math>

The ''I''-adic completion of an ''R''-module ''M'' is the inverse limit of the quotients

: <math>\widehat{M}_I=\varprojlim (M/I^n M).</math>

This procedure converts any module over ''R'' into a complete [[topological module]] over <math>\widehat{R}_I</math>  if ''I'' is finitely generated.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/05GG|title=Stacks Project — Tag 05GG|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu|access-date=2025-05-14}}</ref>

== Examples ==

* The ring of [[p-adic integers|''p''-adic integers]] <math>\Z_p</math> is obtained by completing the ring <math>\Z</math> of integers at the ideal (''p'').

* Let ''R'' = ''K''[''x''<sub>1</sub>,...,''x''<sub>''n''</sub>] be the [[polynomial ring]] in ''n'' variables over a field ''K'' and <math>\mathfrak{m}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> be the maximal ideal generated by the variables. Then the completion <math>\widehat{R}_{\mathfrak{m}}</math> is the ring ''K''[[''x''<sub>1</sub>,...,''x''<sub>''n''</sub>]] of [[formal power series]] in ''n'' variables over ''K''.

* Given a noetherian ring <math>R</math> and an ideal <math>I = (f_1,\ldots, f_n),</math> the <math>I</math>-adic completion of <math>R</math> is an image of a formal power series ring, specifically, the image of the surjection<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0316|title=Stacks Project — Tag 0316|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu|access-date=2017-01-14}}</ref>
::<math>\begin{cases} R[[x_1, \ldots, x_n]] \to \widehat{R}_I \\ x_i \mapsto f_i \end{cases}</math>
:The kernel is the ideal <math>(x_1 - f_1, \ldots, x_n - f_n).</math>

Completions can also be used to analyze the local structure of [[Singularity theory|singularities]] of a [[Scheme (mathematics)|scheme]]. For example, the affine schemes associated to <math>\Complex[x,y]/(xy)</math> and the nodal cubic [[plane curve]] <math>\Complex[x,y]/(y^2 - x^2(1+x))</math> have similar looking singularities at the origin when viewing their graphs (both look like a plus sign). Notice that in the second case, any [[Zariski topology|Zariski neighborhood]] of the origin is still an irreducible curve. If we use completions, then we are looking at a "small enough" neighborhood where the node has two components. Taking the localizations of these rings along the ideal <math>(x,y)</math> and completing gives <math>\Complex[[x,y]]/(xy)</math> and <math>\Complex[[x,y]]/((y+u)(y-u))</math> respectively, where <math>u</math> is the formal square root of <math>x^2(1+x)</math> in <math>\Complex[[x,y]].</math> More explicitly, the power series:

:<math>u = x\sqrt{1+x} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n(2n)!}{(1-2n)(n!)^2(4^n)}x^{n+1}.</math>

Since both rings are given by the intersection of two ideals generated by a homogeneous degree 1 polynomial, we can see algebraically that the singularities "look" the same. This is because such a scheme is the union of two non-equal linear subspaces of the affine plane.

== Properties ==
* The completion of a Noetherian ring with respect to some ideal is a Noetherian ring.<ref>{{harvnb|Atiyah|Macdonald|1969|loc=Theorem 10.26.}}</ref>
* The completion of a Noetherian local ring with respect to the unique maximal ideal is a Noetherian local ring.<ref>{{harvnb|Atiyah|Macdonald|1969|loc=Proposition 10.16. and Theorem 10.26.}}</ref>
* The completion is a functorial operation: a continuous map <math>f\colon R\to S</math> of topological rings gives rise to a map of their completions, <math display=block>\widehat{f}: \widehat{R}\to\widehat{S}.</math>
: Moreover, if <math>M</math> and <math>N</math> are two modules over the same topological ring <math>R</math> and <math>f\colon M\to N</math> is a continuous module map, then <math>f</math> uniquely extends to the map of the completions:
: <math>\widehat{f}: \widehat{M}\to\widehat{N},</math>
: where <math>\widehat{M},\widehat{N}</math> are modules over <math>\widehat{R}.</math>
* The completion of a [[Noetherian ring]] <math>R</math> is a [[flat module]] over <math>R</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Atiyah|Macdonald|1969|loc=Proposition 10.14.}}</ref>
* The completion of a finitely generated module <math>M</math> over a Noetherian ring <math>R</math> can be obtained by ''extension of scalars'':
:: <math> \widehat{M}=M\otimes_R \widehat{R}.</math>
: Together with the previous property, this implies that the functor of completion on finitely generated <math>R</math>-modules is [[exact functor|exact]]: it preserves [[short exact sequence]]s. In particular, taking quotients of rings commutes with completion, meaning that for any quotient <math>R</math>-algebra <math>R / I</math>, there is an isomorphism
:: <math>\widehat{R / I} \cong \widehat R / \widehat I.</math>
* '''[[Cohen structure theorem]]''' (equicharacteristic case). Let <math>R</math> be a complete [[local ring|local]] Noetherian commutative ring with maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> and [[residue field]] <math>\mathbb k</math>. If <math>R</math> contains a field, then
:: <math>R\simeq \mathbb k[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]]/I</math>
: for some <math>n</math> and some ideal <math>I</math> (Eisenbud, Theorem 7.7).
